newsitem.title: UK: Traders cautiously welcome TOCOM aluminium market.
newsitem.headline: Traders cautiously welcome TOCOM aluminium market.

text.p: The Tokyo Commodity Exchange's (TOCOM) ambitious plan to launch a yen-based aluminium futures market next April has been welcomed with cautious optimism by metal traders during LME week in London.
"I'd like to give credit to the TOCOM's ambition to introduce new contracts," an aluminium trader of a major trade house said.
"But our stance is we're ready to trade the new contract if there's enough liquidity."

The TOCOM, which is one of the largest commodity futures markets in Japan, plans to launch the yen-based aluminium futures contract next April, in an attempt to provide Japanese end-users with a price risk hedging tool.

Japan has been forced to cut its aluminium smelting facilities gradually since the 1970s because of high energy costs. Aluminium product makers import almost all their requirements of the metal through long-term contracts with overseas producers and from the spot market.
"Opening an aluminium futures market in Japan sounds logical, given its huge consumption," another aluminium trader said.
"But Japanese users depend on the LME as the risk hedging tool and has no problem. I'm not sure how the TOCOM can attract orders," the trader in London said.
The Japan Aluminium Federation, an industry body of local aluminium product makers, has opposed the TOCOM plan, saying the new futures contract will make local aluminium prices complicated.

Despite the cautious voices, the TOCOM is keen to go ahead and is reminding players of the Sumitomo copper scandal. "The Japanese Aluminium Federation insisted the LME is a perfect risk hedging tool and there's no need to have another market here," Naozo Mabuchi, the TOCOM president, said earlier in Tokyo. "But the Sumitomo copper scandal revealed that the LME is not perfect and has some problems," he told Reuters.

Sumitomo annonced on September 19 that its estimated losses from unauthorised copper trading, stemming from deals by former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka, had risen to $2.6 billion, up from its initial estimate in June of $1.8 billion.
